questions.prompt: The law \(u = -K\hat{x}\) is applied, and the observer model matches the plant. The eigenvalues of the joint system are
questions.explanation: In error coordinates the joint matrix is block triangular, with \(A-BK\) and \(A-LC\) on the diagonal, so the spectra combine. Hiding \(L\) would be true of the reference transfer function, not of the eigenvalues. The open-loop \(A\) is what both gains are there to change. \(KC\) and \(LB\) are not the closed-loop blocks.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a block-triangular closed loop</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">A-BK   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">*   A-LC</text></svg>

options: the eigenvalues of \(A-BK\) together with the eigenvalues of \(A-LC\)
only the eigenvalues of \(A-BK\), because \(L\) is hidden inside the observer
the eigenvalues of \(A\), unchanged by either gain
the eigenvalues of \(KC\) and of \(LB\)

questions.prompt: The regulator poles are \(-2\) and \(-3\). The observer poles are \(-8\) and \(-10\). The sum of all four real parts is
questions.explanation: The joint spectrum is the union, so the real parts add: \(-2-3-8-10 = -23\). Adding only the regulator pair gives \(-5\). Adding only the observer pair gives \(-18\). The product of the observer poles is \(80\), which is not a sum of real parts.

questions.prompt: A scalar plant has \(A = 2\), \(B = 1\), \(K = 5\), \(C = 1\), and \(L = 6\). In the monic polynomial whose roots are the two closed-loop eigenvalues, the coefficient of \(s\) is
questions.explanation: The eigenvalues are \(2 - 5 = -3\) and \(2 - 6 = -4\). The polynomial is \((s+3)(s+4) = s^2 + 7s + 12\), so the coefficient of \(s\) is 7. The constant term \(12\) is the product. Either eigenvalue alone is one factor, not the sum. The open-loop value \(2\) is neither root.

questions.figure_alt: A plant block with a gain K returned and subtracted.

questions.prompt: A scalar observer uses \(\dot{\hat{x}} = a\hat{x} + b u + l(y - c\hat{x})\). Write the eigenvalue of the estimation error in the names \(a\), \(l\), and \(c\).
questions.explanation: The error \(\tilde{x} = x - \hat{x}\) satisfies \(\dot{\tilde{x}} = (a - l c)\tilde{x}\) when the model matches, so the eigenvalue is \(a - l c\). The form \(a + l c\) is the sign error from adding the residual. The form \(a - l\) drops the output coefficient. The control gain is not in this eigenvalue.

questions.figure_alt: A model block with a gain L returned and subtracted.

questions.prompt: A scalar plant has \(A = -1\), \(B = 2\), and \(K = 3\). The state-feedback eigenvalue of \(A - BK\) is
questions.explanation: \(-1 - 2 \times 3 = -7\). Forgetting the input coefficient \(2\) gives \(-1 - 3 = -4\). Using \(A + BK\) gives \(-1 + 6 = 5\), the unstable sign error. Reporting \(K = 3\) reports the gain, not the eigenvalue.

questions.figure_alt: A plant block with a gain K returned and subtracted.

questions.prompt: Put these design steps in the order you would use them for output feedback through an estimate.
questions.explanation: Each gain is designed for its own matrix, and neither design needs the other number. The law then uses the estimate, and the observer has to see the command that the plant sees, or the error equation picks up a leftover input. The eigenvalue check is last: it confirms the triangular split rather than creating it.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a block-triangular closed loop</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">A-BK   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">*   A-LC</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 block matrix with A minus B K and A minus L C on the diagonal.
steps: Place the state-feedback gain from the regulator poles.
Place the observer gain from the error poles.
Replace the state in the control law by the estimate.
Drive the observer with the applied command and with the measured output.
Check that the joint eigenvalues are the union of the two sets you placed.

questions.prompt: The observer model matches the plant, and both gains have been placed. One step is wrong.
questions.explanation: With a matching model the error equation is not driven by the reference, so the transfer function from the reference to the output does not contain the observer poles. They are still eigenvalues, and a nonzero initial estimation error does show them in \(y\). The third step confuses those two facts. The other steps are the split and its hypothesis.

steps: The control law uses the estimate, \(u = -K\hat{x}\).
The joint eigenvalues are those of \(A-BK\) and those of \(A-LC\).
Those observer eigenvalues appear in the transfer function from the reference to the output.
A mismatch between the observer model and the plant removes this clean split.
reasons: A matching model keeps the reference out of the error equation, so the reference transfer does not contain the observer poles.
Observer poles are cancelled only when the model is wrong.
The reference transfer contains every joint eigenvalue, with no cancellation.

questions.prompt: The split into \(A-BK\) and \(A-LC\) fails to stay that simple when
questions.explanation: The triangular form uses one \(A\) and one \(C\) in both the plant and the copy. A different model leaves a driving term in the error, and the characteristic polynomial does not factor so cleanly. Who designed the gains is irrelevant. Faster observer poles are a common choice, not a threat to the algebra. Dimension \(2\) is ordinary.

options: the two gains were designed by different people
the observer is built from a different \(A\) or \(C\) than the plant
the observer poles are faster than the regulator poles

questions.prompt: Which statements hold when the observer model matches the plant?
questions.explanation: Separate placement is the content of the principle, and the spectrum is the union. Nothing forces the two sets to coincide. A wrong model is exactly the case where the extra cross term appears and the split is no longer the whole story.

options: \(K\) and \(L\) may be placed separately.
The joint eigenvalues are the union of the two placed sets.
The observer poles have to equal the regulator poles.
A wrong model in the observer keeps the same split.

questions.prompt: Regulator poles \(-1\) and \(-4\), observer poles \(-6\) and \(-6\). The sum of the four real parts, which the joint system must show, is
questions.explanation: Union means addition of the real parts: \(-1-4-6-6 = -17\). The regulator pair alone sums to \(-5\). The repeated observer pole is \(-6\), not \(-12\), until you count it twice. The product \(24\) of the regulator poles is not this sum.

questions.prompt: A feedforward term from the reference is added on top of \(u = -K\hat{x}\). The eigenvalues of \(A-BK\) and \(A-LC\)
questions.explanation: A term \(F r\) enters as an input. It does not change \(A-BK\) or \(A-LC\). Those matrices are the homogeneous part. The feedforward gain is a matrix of a different shape, and it is not a list of eigenvalues. Collapsing the spectrum would mean deleting \(K\), which this term does not do.

collapse to the observer poles only
stay where the two gains put them
become the eigenvalues of the feedforward gain

questions.prompt: After \(K\) and \(L\) are placed for a matching model, a constant reference still needs
questions.explanation: Pole placement fixes the transient. The steady gain from \(r\) to \(y\) is a separate number, the feedforward or reference scale in the command. A second copy of \(K\) does not create that path. Matching the two pole sets, or setting \(L = K\), is not required for a constant reference.
